subtitle: "The Baghdád period, 1853–1863"
toc: true

::: {.lead}
The Kitáb-i-Íqán was not written in tranquillity. It belongs to a decade of exile that began
with a community in ruins and ended with Bahá'u'lláh's declaration of His Mission — and the
Book was revealed near the close of it, on the eve of that declaration.
:::

## Before the exile

The Báb declared His Mission in Shíráz in 1844. Within six years He had been executed in
Tabríz, and the movement He founded was being hunted across Persia.

In August 1852 two Bábís, acting on their own and against the explicit teaching of their Faith,
attempted to assassinate Náṣiri'd-Dín Sháh. The reprisal fell on the whole community.
Bahá'u'lláh, though innocent and in fact widely known to oppose such acts, was arrested and
confined for four months in the Síyáh-Chál — the Black Pit, an abandoned underground reservoir
beneath Ṭihrán, where He was held in chains among criminals.

It was in that dungeon that He received the first intimations of His own Revelation. Nothing in
the Íqán can be read apart from this: the Book's author had already been given the thing He was
not yet free to announce.

## Banishment to 'Iráq

The Russian minister intervened on His behalf, and testimony from fellow prisoners established
His innocence. He was released, then banished.

::: {.timeline}
- **12 January 1853** Departs Ṭihrán for Baghdád in midwinter, accompanied by His family, including His nine-year-old son ʻAbdu'l-Bahá.
- **8 April 1853** Arrives in Baghdád.
:::

What He found there was a wreck. Shoghi Effendi describes a community reduced to "no more than a
handful of souls, faint and dispirited." Leaderless since the Báb's execution, it had fractured:
by one count some twenty-five individuals had put themselves forward as the Promised One.

Mírzá Yaḥyá, Bahá'u'lláh's half-brother, had been nominated by the Báb as the community's
nominal head. He spent these years in concealment, and — with Siyyid Muḥammad of Isfahán —
worked to undermine Bahá'u'lláh's growing influence.

## The withdrawal to Kurdistán

Rather than contend with His half-brother and split the community further, Bahá'u'lláh left.

::: {.timeline}
- **10 April 1854** Departs Baghdád alone, telling no one, under the name Darvísh Muḥammad.
- **1854–1856** Lives in austere seclusion in the mountains of Kurdistán, near Sulaymáníyyah.
- **19 March 1856** Returns to Baghdád after two years, at the community's urging.
:::

He had intended to remain unknown. But His learning drew the attention of Kurdish and Sunní
divines of the region, who sought Him out — and word of the remarkable dervish eventually
reached Baghdád, where His family recognized the description.

## The years of revival

The seven years between His return and His final banishment are the most productive of the
Baghdád period, and the ones that matter most for reading the Íqán.

A modest house in the Karkh quarter became a place of resort. Visitors came from across the
region and across religions — Kurds, Persians, Arabs and Turks; Muslims, Jews and Christians;
ʻulamá and Persian nobility among them. The British consul-general, Colonel Kemball, went so far
as to offer Bahá'u'lláh British citizenship and to convey any message He wished to Queen Victoria.
He declined.

The Writings of these years include the **Hidden Words** (1274 A.H.), the **Seven Valleys** — His
principal mystical work — and the **Four Valleys**. The Kitáb-i-Íqán came near the end, in
1278 A.H./1862.

## The occasion of the Book

Ḥájí Mírzá Siyyid Muḥammad, the eldest maternal uncle of the Báb, had never accepted his Nephew
as the Promised One of Islám. Certain traditions concerning the Qá'im seemed to him unfulfilled.
Persuaded by a fellow believer to put his difficulties directly to Bahá'u'lláh, he travelled to
'Iráq — ostensibly on pilgrimage to the Shrines at Karbilá and Najaf — and attained His presence
in Baghdád.

Bahá'u'lláh asked him to go home, consider carefully, and return with his questions written
down. Within two days and two nights, the answer was revealed.

The Book was also written in fulfillment of a prophecy of the Báb: that the Promised One would
complete the text of the unfinished Persian Bayán.

## What followed

Bahá'u'lláh's renown was precisely the problem. Shaykh ʻAbdu'l-Ḥusayn and the Persian
consul-general Mírzá Buzurg Khán pressed against Him; the Persian government in turn pressed
the Ottoman authorities to move Him further from its borders.

::: {.timeline}
- **Spring 1863** Ottoman authorities order His removal to Constantinople.
- **22 April 1863** Leaves His house and enters the Najíbíyyih Garden — the Garden of Riḍván — where He declares His Mission to His companions.
- **3 May 1863** Sets out for Constantinople after twelve days in the Garden.
:::

The Íqán, revealed the year before, was written by One whose station was known to Himself and to
a few, and not yet proclaimed. It answers a seeker's questions about how to recognize a
Manifestation of God — and it was written by a Manifestation of God awaiting the hour to speak.
